questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index
questions.stem: This plot shows a single drug's effect increasing with its concentration on a log scale, leveling off at a maximum. What type of dose-response relationship does it represent?

explanation.summary: A graded dose-response curve plots the continuous magnitude of drug effect against drug concentration for a single patient, rising sigmoidally to a maximum (Emax) with the half-maximal effect defining the EC50.
explanation.whyCorrect: A graded dose-response curve plots the continuous magnitude of drug effect against drug concentration for a single patient, rising sigmoidally to a maximum (Emax) with the half-maximal effect defining the EC50.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A log-kill curve plots surviving tumor cell fraction against chemotherapy cycles, not effect versus concentration.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A quantal curve plots the percentage of a population showing an all-or-none response, not the continuous effect magnitude in one system.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A time-concentration curve plots drug level against time, a pharmacokinetic plot rather than an effect plot.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A cumulative frequency distribution is how quantal data are displayed across a population, not a single drug's graded effect.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index
questions.stem: This bell-shaped frequency plot shows the number of patients responding at each dose, with the central peak (mu) marked. Which pharmacodynamic parameter does that central/median value define?

explanation.summary: A quantal dose-effect frequency curve is a normal (Gaussian) distribution; the dose at its center, where 50% of the population shows the defined all-or-none response, is the median effective dose, ED50.
explanation.whyCorrect: A quantal dose-effect frequency curve is a normal (Gaussian) distribution; the dose at its center, where 50% of the population shows the defined all-or-none response, is the median effective dose, ED50.

whyWrongByChoice.A: TD50 is the median dose producing a toxic effect, which comes from a separate toxicity distribution, not the therapeutic response peak.
whyWrongByChoice.C: EC50 is the concentration giving half-maximal effect on a graded curve in one system, not the median of a population frequency plot.
whyWrongByChoice.D: LD50 is the median lethal dose, determined from death as the endpoint in animal studies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Therapeutic index is a ratio such as TD50/ED50 that compares two curves, not a single central value on one distribution.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index
questions.stem: This figure shows two sigmoidal curves, one for efficacy and one for toxicity, plotted against log drug concentration. A drug whose two curves are farther apart on this axis is best described as having what property?

explanation.summary: The greater the separation between the efficacy and toxicity curves, the larger the therapeutic index and the safer the drug, because effective and toxic doses overlap less.
explanation.whyCorrect: The greater the separation between the efficacy and toxicity curves, the larger the therapeutic index and the safer the drug, because effective and toxic doses overlap less.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Half-life describes how fast a drug is eliminated and has no bearing on how far apart the efficacy and toxicity curves lie.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Maximal efficacy is the height of the efficacy curve's plateau, not its separation from the toxicity curve.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Onset of action depends on route and absorption kinetics, not on the concentration gap between benefit and harm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Potency is the position of the efficacy curve along the concentration axis, independent of where the toxicity curve sits.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index
questions.stem: This figure plots therapeutic, toxic, and lethal effect curves with ED50, TD50, and LD50 marked. What quantity is obtained by dividing the lethal median dose by the effective median dose shown here?

explanation.summary: The therapeutic index is the ratio of a dose producing toxicity/lethality to a dose producing the desired effect (e.g., LD50/ED50 or TD50/ED50); a larger ratio indicates a safer drug.
explanation.whyCorrect: The therapeutic index is the ratio of a dose producing toxicity/lethality to a dose producing the desired effect (e.g., LD50/ED50 or TD50/ED50); a larger ratio indicates a safer drug.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Maximal efficacy (Emax) is the plateau of a graded dose-response curve, not a ratio of two doses.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A potency ratio compares equi-effective doses of two different drugs, not lethal and effective doses of the same drug.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bioavailability is the fraction of an administered dose reaching the systemic circulation, a pharmacokinetic measure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Margin of safety is usually defined from curve extremes, such as LD1/ED99, rather than the ratio of median doses.

questions.stem: This diagram shows aspirin acetylating a serine residue on two related enzymes. Acetylation permanently inactivates the upper enzyme, but for the lower enzyme it does not abolish function — it switches the enzyme to a new catalytic activity. What new activity does the acetylated lower enzyme acquire?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peroxidase-only activity with no lipid product

explanation.summary: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates a serine in the active site of COX-1, fully inactivating it. For COX-2, the same acetylation does not stop the enzyme but converts its cyclooxygenase activity into a lipoxygenase (LOX) activity, generating anti-inflammatory lipoxins rather than prostaglandins.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates a serine in the active site of COX-1, fully inactivating it. For COX-2, the same acetylation does not stop the enzyme but converts its cyclooxygenase activity into a lipoxygenase (LOX) activity, generating anti-inflammatory lipoxins rather than prostaglandins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetylation never enhances cyclooxygenase activity; it blocks prostaglandin formation in both enzymes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid from membranes upstream of COX and is a separate enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thromboxane synthase is a distinct platelet enzyme acting on PGH2, and aspirin reduces thromboxane production.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Acetylated COX-2 still produces a lipid product, 15R-HETE, which leukocytes convert to aspirin-triggered lipoxins.

questions.stem: This schematic traces how diverse stimuli lead through arachidonic acid to a family of tissue-specific products. The product shown at the far right is generated chiefly by platelets. What is its principal physiologic action?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inhibits platelet aggregation and causes vasodilation

explanation.summary: The rightmost branch product is Thromboxane A2 (TxA2), synthesized largely by platelets. TxA2 is a potent promoter of platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction, which is why aspirin's inhibition of its synthesis produces an antithrombotic effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: The rightmost branch product is Thromboxane A2 (TxA2), synthesized largely by platelets. TxA2 is a potent promoter of platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction, which is why aspirin's inhibition of its synthesis produces an antithrombotic effect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gastric acid secretion is driven by histamine, gastrin and acetylcholine; prostaglandins actually inhibit acid and protect the mucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Inhibiting aggregation and causing vasodilation are actions of prostacyclin (PGI2) from endothelium, which opposes thromboxane.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thromboxane A2 constricts airway smooth muscle; bronchodilation is attributed to PGE2.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal sodium excretion is promoted by PGE2 and PGI2 in the kidney, not by platelet-derived thromboxane.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics: Volume of Distribution and Elimination Kinetics
questions.stem: This plasma drug concentration versus time plot is a straight, linearly declining line. What elimination kinetics does this pattern represent?

explanation.summary: A constant absolute amount of drug removed per unit time, independent of concentration, yields a straight line on a linear plot, characteristic of zero-order kinetics.
explanation.whyCorrect: A constant absolute amount of drug removed per unit time, independent of concentration, yields a straight line on a linear plot, characteristic of zero-order kinetics.

whyWrongByChoice.A: First-order elimination removes a constant fraction per unit time, giving an exponential curve on a linear axis rather than a straight line.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Enterohepatic recirculation creates secondary peaks or bumps on the concentration curve, not a straight decline.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Flow-limited elimination applies to high-extraction drugs and still follows first-order exponential decay.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Absorption kinetics shape the rising phase; the declining straight line reflects elimination, not absorption.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics: Volume of Distribution and Elimination Kinetics
questions.stem: This schematic shows a constant 2.5 units/h of drug removed at every concentration step. Which drug is a classic clinical example of this saturable elimination pattern?

explanation.summary: Ethanol (along with phenytoin and aspirin at high doses) is eliminated at a constant amount per unit time because its metabolic pathway is saturated, defining zero-order kinetics.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ethanol (along with phenytoin and aspirin at high doses) is eliminated at a constant amount per unit time because its metabolic pathway is saturated, defining zero-order kinetics.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Penicillin is eliminated by first-order renal tubular secretion, with a constant fraction cleared per unit time.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Metoprolol is cleared by CYP2D6 with first-order kinetics at therapeutic doses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gentamicin is renally filtered with first-order elimination proportional to concentration and renal function.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Digoxin is renally excreted with first-order kinetics and a long, constant half-life of about 36-40 hours.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics: Volume of Distribution and Elimination Kinetics
questions.stem: On a linear y-axis, this plasma concentration versus time curve declines exponentially rather than as a straight line. What does the exponential shape indicate about elimination?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An increasing fraction is eliminated as concentration falls

choices.label: B
choices.text: Drug is eliminated only above a threshold concentration

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elimination stops once concentration reaches half the peak

choices.label: D
choices.text: A constant fraction of drug is eliminated per unit time

choices.label: E
choices.text: A constant absolute amount of drug is eliminated per unit time

explanation.summary: First-order kinetics removes a constant proportion of drug per unit time, so the elimination rate is proportional to concentration and the curve decays exponentially on a linear scale.
explanation.whyCorrect: First-order kinetics removes a constant proportion of drug per unit time, so the elimination rate is proportional to concentration and the curve decays exponentially on a linear scale.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An increasing fraction eliminated as concentration falls has no standard kinetic basis; first-order removes the same fraction at every concentration.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Threshold-dependent elimination is not a recognized kinetic order and would not produce smooth exponential decay.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Elimination continues past half the peak; each successive half-life removes another half of what remains.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A constant absolute amount per unit time defines zero-order kinetics, which gives a straight line on a linear plot.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics: Volume of Distribution and Elimination Kinetics
questions.stem: In this schematic the elimination rate halves as concentration halves (5 to 2.5 to 1.25 units/h). What quantity remains constant across all concentrations for such a drug?

choices.label: C
choices.text: The absolute amount of drug eliminated per hour

choices.label: D
choices.text: The fraction of drug bound to plasma protein

choices.label: E
choices.text: The time required to eliminate the entire dose

explanation.summary: Because a constant proportion is removed per unit time, the time for concentration to fall by half is fixed regardless of the starting concentration, so half-life is constant in first-order kinetics.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because a constant proportion is removed per unit time, the time for concentration to fall by half is fixed regardless of the starting concentration, so half-life is constant in first-order kinetics.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Maximum elimination capacity is approached only in zero-order kinetics; here the rate changes with concentration, so the drug is well below that capacity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The absolute amount eliminated per hour falls as concentration falls (5, then 2.5, then 1.25), so it is not constant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protein binding fraction is a distribution property that is not shown here and does not define first-order elimination.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Time to eliminate the whole dose grows with dose; in first-order kinetics roughly 4-5 half-lives are needed to clear about 94-97%.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics: Volume of Distribution and Elimination Kinetics
questions.stem: This graph compares steady-state acetaminophen concentrations for three formulations. The intravenous curve is nearly flat while the oral curves oscillate between peaks and troughs. What best explains the flat intravenous profile?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Intravenous drug bypasses steady state entirely

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intravenous dosing uses a far larger total dose

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intravenous drug is not subject to first-order elimination

choices.label: D
choices.text: Continuous infusion delivers drug at a rate matching elimination

choices.label: E
choices.text: Intravenous drug has a much shorter half-life

explanation.summary: A continuous IV infusion inputs drug at a constant rate equal to the elimination rate at steady state, so concentration plateaus without the peak-trough swings seen with intermittent oral dosing.
explanation.whyCorrect: A continuous IV infusion inputs drug at a constant rate equal to the elimination rate at steady state, so concentration plateaus without the peak-trough swings seen with intermittent oral dosing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IV infusions still approach steady state over about 4-5 half-lives; the flat line is the steady-state plateau, not a bypass of it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A larger total dose would raise the average concentration but would not by itself remove peak-trough fluctuation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acetaminophen is eliminated by first-order kinetics regardless of route at therapeutic doses.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Half-life is a property of the drug and patient, not the route; a shorter half-life would increase fluctuation, not flatten it.
